html:
The trial of Socrates took place in Athens in 399 BCE. A jury of 501 citizens found the philosopher Socrates guilty of impiety and of corrupting the young, and sentenced him to death.

His accusers, led by Meletus and the democratic politician Anytus, said he did not honour the city's gods, brought in new ones and led young men astray. Behind the charges lay politics. Athens had just lost the Peloponnesian War, and two men linked with Socrates had done the city great harm: Alcibiades, and Critias, leader of the Thirty Tyrants. An amnesty barred charges over the Thirty, so religion served instead. Comedies like The Clouds had long painted him as a dangerous clever talker.

He was convicted by a fairly narrow margin. Asked to propose a penalty, he suggested free meals at public expense, as a benefactor of the city. The jury chose death. He refused his friends' plan to escape and drank hemlock in prison.

The trial shaped Western thought. Plato wrote the Apology, Crito and Phaedo about it, and Xenophon wrote his own defence of Socrates. It still raises the question of how a democracy treats people who question it.
